questions.prompt: Which are the four classes of test data used in this lesson?
questions.explanation: Designing data in valid, invalid, boundary and special classes makes sure you exercise normal use, rejection, edges and awkward real-world values.

questions.prompt: A 'Nights' field accepts 1 to 30. Which value is an invalid-partition value?
questions.explanation: 31 is just outside the upper boundary. 1 and 30 are valid boundaries; 15 is a typical valid value.

questions.prompt: Recording the purpose of each test data row (for example 'upper boundary') makes the data easier to review and maintain.
questions.explanation: A purpose column explains why a value exists, so reviewers can spot gaps and maintainers do not delete important edge cases.

questions.prompt: Which values are 'special' test data for a surname field? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Apostrophes, accented characters and hyphens are legitimate names that commonly break validation, encoding or SQL. 'Smith' is plain valid data.

questions.prompt: Tests pass alone but fail when run together because two tests both register 'test@example.com'. What is the best fix?
options: Run tests in a fixed order
Make each test create unique data (e.g. a generated suffix) and clean up after itself
Remove the uniqueness rule in the test environment
questions.explanation: Independent tests own their data. Ordering and retries hide the problem, and turning off the uniqueness rule means you no longer test real behaviour.

questions.prompt: When is masked production data the right choice over synthetic data?
options: Always, because it is more realistic
When realistic distributions or complex relationships are hard to synthesise, and only with approval and proper anonymisation
When the tester is in a hurry
questions.explanation: Synthetic data is preferred. Masked production data can be justified for realism, but only under approval and with irreversible anonymisation.

questions.prompt: How many test cases does pytest collect from this parametrised test?
questions.explanation: parametrize creates one test case per tuple in the list; there are four tuples, so four test cases are collected.

questions.prompt: A team copies the full production customer database into a shared test environment that contractors can access. What is the strongest recommendation?
options: It is fine because contractors signed an NDA
Stop: replace it with synthetic data, or masked data with irreversible anonymisation and approval, because unmasked personal data in test breaks privacy obligations and widens exposure
Encrypt the test laptops and continue
questions.explanation: Data protection rules apply to test environments too. Deleting one field is not anonymisation, and NDAs or laptop encryption do not remove the risk of exposing real personal data.

questions.prompt: A booking test uses check-in date '2026-11-20' hard-coded. It passed for months, then started failing on 21 November 2026 with 'date must be in the future'. What is the best fix?
options: Compute dates relative to today (e.g. today + 7 days) so the data stays valid whenever the test runs
Disable the future-date rule in test
questions.explanation: Time-dependent data must be relative. Moving the hard-coded date only postpones the same failure; disabling the rule removes real behaviour.

coding.title: Generate 3-value boundary values
coding.prompt:
Write `boundary_values(lo, hi)` for an integer field that accepts `lo` to `hi` inclusive.

Return a dict with two sorted lists, using **3-value BVA** (each boundary plus the values just inside and just outside):
- `"valid"`: values from `{lo, lo+1, hi-1, hi}` (no duplicates)
- `"invalid"`: `[lo-1, hi+1]`

Example: `boundary_values(1, 30)` returns `{"valid": [1, 2, 29, 30], "invalid": [0, 31]}`.

Edge case: when `lo == hi`, valid is just `[lo]`.
coding.explanation: A set removes duplicates when the range is tiny (for example 1..2 gives the same values for lo+1 and hi). Filtering keeps only values inside the range, and the two invalid values sit one step outside each boundary.
hints: The invalid values are always one below `lo` and one above `hi`.
Put the four candidate valid values in a set to remove duplicates.
Filter with `lo <= v <= hi` and `sorted(...)` the result.

coding.title: Classify name test data
coding.explanation: The checks run in priority order: invalid first, then boundary lengths, then special characters. Trimming first matches the rule and catches the 'only spaces' case, which is a classic invalid value.
hints: Trim with `.strip()` before measuring the length.
Check invalid, then boundary, then special, in that order.
`string.ascii_letters` lets you test whether each character is a plain letter.

tests.name: plain and special names
tests.code:
assert classify_name("Asha") == "valid"
assert classify_name("O'Brien") == "special"
assert classify_name("Zoë") == "special"

tests.name: boundaries
tests.code:
assert classify_name("A") == "boundary"
assert classify_name("b" * 50) == "boundary"
assert classify_name("  " + "c" * 50 + " ") == "boundary"
